title: From Gadar to Dhurandhar: How Bollywood Reshaped India's Language of Patriotism
excerpt: As India celebrates its 80th Independence Day, a look at how Hindi cinema evolved from sloganeering war dramas to grounded, commercially dominant nationalist blockbusters.
body:
• Bollywood's patriotic genre has undergone a major transformation — from sloganeering war films like Gadar and Border to grounded blockbusters like Dhurandhar (₹894 crore) and Border 2 (₹323 crore).
  • Trade experts say the shift is driven by audiences demanding real storytelling over patriotic speeches, with younger viewers expecting strong characters and production values.
  • The 2026 Independence Day weekend sees the release of Love and War (Sanjay Leela Bhansali) and Naagzilla, reflecting Bollywood's continued investment in the patriotic-adjacent calendar.
  • Films like Swades and Rang De Basanti have shaped how the diaspora thinks about its relationship with India, making the genre deeply personal for NRIs.

The Old Guard: Patriotism as Spectacle

For decades, Bollywood's approach to patriotism followed a familiar playbook. Films like Gadar: Ek Prem Katha (2001) gave audiences Sunny Deol uprooting a hand pump while declaring "Hindustan Zindabad Tha, Zindabad Hai, Zindabad Rahega." JP Dutta's Border (1997) recreated the Battle of Longewala. These were crowd-pleasers built around rousing speeches, enemy-across-the-border narratives, and emotional patriotic songs.

https://x.com/ani_digital/status/2088491108439650414

The template worked. Films like Uri: The Surgical Strike (₹245 crore) and The Kashmir Files (₹252 crore) proved that nationalist themes could deliver breakout box-office numbers. But industry observers say the formula also led to genre saturation, with too many similar films arriving alongside action hits like Baby and Airlift and biopics like The Accidental Prime Minister.

The New Wave: Grounded Storytelling at Scale

The success of Dhurandhar and Border 2 in 2025-26 has rewritten the commercial rules. Dhurandhar, directed by Aditya Dhar and starring Ranveer Singh, collected ₹894 crore — putting it in the ₹1,000 crore club conversation. Border 2, released on the Republic Day weekend with an ensemble cast including Sunny Deol, Varun Dhawan, and Diljit Dosanjh, earned ₹323 crore.

"A film like Dhurandhar avoids long speeches and sticks to a tight, believable story. These films now blend genres — Border 2 isn't just a war movie; it's about friendship, teamwork and loss."

— Bhuvanesh Mendiratta, Managing Director, Miraj Entertainment

Trade experts attribute the leap to three factors. First, grounded tone — less drama, more realism. Second, genre-blending that makes war films work as relationship dramas. Third, production values and strong music that pull audiences from tier-2 and tier-3 cities into theatres.

Devang Sampat, managing director of Cinépolis India, noted that Indian cinema is "increasingly claiming the format-driven, spectacle-first space traditionally associated with Hollywood tentpoles," with strong audience response in premium formats like 4DX.

The Diaspora Connection

For NRI audiences, the patriotic genre has always carried a different weight. Films like Swades (2004), where Shah Rukh Khan's NRI scientist returns to help a rural village, and Chak De! India (2007), with its themes of proving loyalty to India, speak directly to the diaspora experience of navigating identity across borders.

Rang De Basanti (2006) connected college-age idealism to freedom-struggle sacrifice, becoming a cultural touchstone for young Indians globally. These films shaped how a generation of diaspora Indians articulated their relationship with the country they left.

Independence Day 2026 at the Box Office

This Independence Day weekend continues the pattern of studios clustering patriotic-adjacent releases around August 15. Sanjay Leela Bhansali's Love and War, starring Ranbir Kapoor, Alia Bhatt, and Vicky Kaushal, explores love against a backdrop of conflict. Naagzilla: Naag Lok Ka Pehla Kaand pairs Kartik Aaryan with Indian mythology in a festive entertainer. Meanwhile, Dhurandhar 2 already released to massive numbers during Eid 2026, and Salman Khan's Battle of Galwan is expected later this year.

"Patriotism is simply the message. It is important to design and curate films meaningfully to fall within the commercial zone."

— Vishek Chauhan, independent exhibitor

What Changed — and What Didn't

The themes still revolve around a cross-border enemy, national pride, and sacrifice. What changed is the filmmaking craft. Earlier war films like Ikkis (₹28 crore) and 120 Bahadur (₹15 crore) underperformed despite patriotic premises because they lacked the commercial instincts of Dhurandhar and Border 2. The audience still wants patriotism — they just want it wrapped in better stories, stronger characters, and a cinematic experience worth leaving home for.
image_caption: Actor Ranveer Singh, whose role in Dhurandhar helped redefine Bollywood's patriotic genre. The film collected ₹894 crore, shifting audience expectations from sloganeering spectacles to grounded storytelling.
